profile.story: Tasha bought out her father's two-truck service company in 2015 and grew it to five trucks doing residential repair, replacement and maintenance plans across the north metro. The work is good and the phone rings; what hurts is that she is still the dispatcher of last resort, the estimator on every replacement over $8K, and the person who decides whether a $400 discount is allowed. Her office manager Renee reshuffles the board by hand every morning because the field app and the schedule never agree. Tasha has not taken more than four days off since 2021 and is starting to resent a business she otherwise likes.

intake.q2: We service, repair and replace residential heating and cooling systems for homeowners in the north metro — about 70% of the work is inside 25 minutes of the shop. Five trucks, two of them replacement crews. Customers find us on Google, through the plumbers and realtors we've worked with for years, and through our maintenance plan members. Everything is delivered by our own W-2 techs; we sub out sheet-metal fabrication and electrical panel upgrades.

P1.note: Five sources named with monthly volume (q23: LSA 46, referrals 31, plan members 28, repeat 12, signs 3); cost known only for the $2,100 Google spend, quality scored from memory.
P1.why_not_higher: Nothing is logged in one place — the field app only holds jobs that booked, so unbooked inquiries are nowhere.

P2.note: Service calls answered within the hour during business hours (q24, confirmed on the board rebuild); replacement callbacks 'same day, sometimes next.' Capture is partial — booked jobs only.
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs every inquiry captured in one system; the ones that don't book are not recorded anywhere.

P3.note: Q24: about 35% of replacement quotes get a second touch, service calls essentially none. No record of who was followed up.
P3.why_not_higher: No defined sequence and no way to see a missed follow-up.

P4.note: Q25: no written process, every tech runs the good/better/best sheet differently; 42% close is an estimate not tracked by source, person or service.
P4.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs a rate that is actually tracked; this one is recalled.

P5.note: Price book on file dated March 2024, built by marking up supply-house cost; diagnostic fee $89 unchanged since 2022 against a $58 loaded tech hour. Discounts are Tasha's call in the moment.
P5.why_not_higher: One change in two years with anecdotal reasoning and no written discount rule is the anchor-1 line exactly.

P6.note: Good/better/best equipment tiers exist on replacement and a $19/mo entry plan; IAQ and duct sealing are offered 'if the tech thinks of it' (q29).
P6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a scripted upsell on the core offer; nothing about the add-on is scripted or expected.

P7.note: Plan roster shows 410 members renewing at 71% and repeat around 55%; the roster also shows roughly 1,100 households with nothing logged in 24+ months. No reactivation has ever run (q27).
P7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the inactive list pulled and worked; it has never been pulled.

P8.note: Q30: marketing is 'me, when I have time', sales is Tasha for replacements; leads, conversion, CAC and value have never been looked at together.
P8.why_not_higher: No named owner for either function and nothing reviewed on a cadence.

P9.note: P&L confirms 42% gross margin company-wide; q17 and the data room confirm no job costing exists, so the 38% replacement / 51% service split in q13 is her estimate.

P10.note: QuickBooks monthlies close 'around the 25th' (q20 monthly-delayed); reviewed when cash feels tight. One revenue target, no margin target by her own answer in q21.

assessment.owner_objective: More profit & cash flow — then Reduce owner dependence, Better operations & delivery capacity
assessment.owner_belief: Honestly I think we just need more trucks and more techs. We turn away work in July and again in January and I feel like I'm leaving money on the table every peak. It's been true for at least three years and it gets worse every summer.
assessment.primary_constraint: Replacement revenue is owner-bound: every quote over about $8,000 waits on Tasha's calendar, so quote speed and follow-through are capped by whatever her week allows — not by truck count.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Replacement quotes go out 2–3 days after the visit; only about a third get a second touch; the loss reason she names unprompted is 'somebody got them a number faster'; the four-week test fails at day nine on quoting; dispatch pulls her back in on top of it.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$50K expected operating profit lost to slow replacement quotes and missing follow-up · ~$19K of office payroll on the 11 weekly hours Renee spends re-keying and chasing · ~312 owner hours a year on quoting and dispatch rescue.
assessment.constraint_fix: Templated replacement pricing the two senior techs can quote from on the spot, a 24-hour quote standard with a three-touch follow-up sequence, and a written discount rule so Tasha is not the only exception path.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Reprice the diagnostic fee and the flat-rate repair book against the $58 loaded tech hour — a decision, not a project, measurable in 30 days and entirely in Tasha's control.

opportunities.title: Answer and follow up the replacement leads that currently die
opportunities.finding: 120 inquiries a month across five sources (built live in b2 from the LSA dashboard and the field app). Replacement callbacks run same-day-to-next-day and only about 35% of quotes get a second touch, so roughly a fifth of the annual lead flow is never worked to a decision. Recovering part of it closes at the rate they already close, on crews that q31 says are not yet at the wall.
opportunities.blueprint: Single inbound number and inbox into the field app, a 24-hour quote standard, and a three-touch sequence (day 1 call, day 3 text with the quote link, day 7 call) that shows an unworked quote on the board.
opportunities.replaces: Renee's memory and Tasha's evening callbacks

opportunities.title: Rebuild the service price book on cost-plus
opportunities.finding: The price book on file is dated March 2024 and was built by marking up supply-house cost; the $89 diagnostic fee has been unchanged since 2022 against a $58 loaded technician hour (q56). The service and repair line is 30% of revenue at a 51% margin — a modest, defensible move on that line only, not on replacement.
opportunities.blueprint: Cost-plus rebuild of the flat-rate book from the loaded rates in q56, a written discount rule at two tiers, and a one-page script so the techs can say the number out loud without calling Tasha.

opportunities.title: Work the dormant household list back onto maintenance plans
opportunities.finding: The plan roster shows roughly 1,100 households with nothing logged in 24 months or more, against 410 current members renewing at 71%. No reactivation has ever run (q27). The range is entered by hand because there is no campaign history to calculate a rate from — the low end assumes a 2% take, the high end 6%, both against the $780 annual plan-member value she quoted in q26.
opportunities.blueprint: Pull the 24-month dormant list out of the field app, segment by last service type, and run a three-message reactivation to plan enrollment with Kara owning the call-backs.
